claims.text: W particles are pre-alloyed with approximately 1–2 wt% Ti and embedded in a Cu matrix.
Vacuum sintering at 1000–1100 °C for 15–30 minutes promotes reactive diffusion at W/Cu interfaces.
Reactive diffusion produces a thin, continuous Ti-based interfacial film between W and Cu.
The proposed interfacial film may consist of TiW or TiCu.
The Ti-based interfacial film lowers W/Cu interfacial energy.
The Ti-based interfacial film enhances Cu wetting of W.
The Ti-based interfacial film acts as a diffusion barrier.
Improved interfacial bonding reduces interfacial void formation.
The controlled interfacial layer reduces phase separation.
Limiting Ti to approximately 1–2 wt% and the hold time to 15–30 minutes avoids excessive intermetallic growth.
The Ti-modified composite will have a lower interfacial void fraction than a conventionally mechanically alloyed W–Cu composite without Ti.
The Ti-modified composite will have better thermal transport than the conventional mechanical-alloying baseline.
The Ti-modified composite will have better mechanical durability under irradiation than the conventional mechanical-alloying baseline.
The conventional mechanical-alloying baseline has higher void content than the proposed Ti-modified material.
The conventional mechanical-alloying baseline has poorer W/Cu interfacial bonding than the proposed Ti-modified material.
Reactive diffusion and intermetallic formation are well documented in analogous material systems.
The precise interfacial phase, layer thickness, and long-term irradiation stability in W–Cu remain uncertain and require experimental validation.
A statistically significant failure to reduce interfacial voids relative to the Ti-free control would falsify the hypothesis.
Inferior thermal conductivity or mechanical performance caused by a thick or brittle interfacial layer would falsify the hypothesis.
